readings.introduction: SQL injection happens when a value supplied by a user becomes part of the statement the database parses. database/sql gives you a second channel: the query text reaches the driver as one string and every argument travels beside it as a typed value. sections.body: Build a statement with + or fmt.Sprintf and the database receives one string. It cannot know which characters came from your code and which came from a form field, so a name such as x' OR '1'='1 closes the string literal and appends a condition that is always true. Escaping quotes by hand looks like a fix until a different character set, a backslash rule or a numeric position that needs no quotes at all defeats it. The durable fix is structural: keep the statement constant and pass values through the driver's parameter mechanism, so a value never passes through the SQL parser as syntax. Placeholder syntax belongs to the driver, not to database/sql: PostgreSQL drivers use $1, $2 and so on, while MySQL and SQLite drivers use ?.

sections.body: A database driver implements a few interfaces from database/sql/driver. This program registers a tiny fake whose connection implements QueryerContext: database/sql calls it with the query string and a slice of driver.NamedValue, and the fake prints both instead of contacting a server. Four calls show a concatenated statement, a parameterized one, an allow-listed ORDER BY and a LIKE search for text that itself contains wildcard characters.

sections.walkthrough: In the first call the attacker's quote marks are inside the sql line and args is empty: the OR clause is now part of the statement. In the second call the statement is constant and the same characters arrive as a string argument bound to $1, so the database compares name with that exact string. database/sql converts each argument to a driver.Value before the driver sees it, which is why the untyped 20 arrives as int64. The sort key is looked up in a map of fixed SQL fragments, so the hostile key never reaches the driver at all. The LIKE pattern is still an argument, but its % and _ were escaped with ! first and the statement declares ESCAPE '!'. The fake parses nothing; it models the interface boundary, not database behavior.

sections.body: A placeholder can stand only where the grammar expects a value. Table names, column names, ASC and DESC are part of the statement's structure, so a database either rejects ORDER BY $1 or sorts every row by the same constant value, which silently does nothing. When a request legitimately chooses among columns, map public keys such as newest or name to SQL fragments written in your code, reject anything else with a 400 and keep the map next to the query so a reviewer sees the complete set. The same rule covers table names chosen for partitioning or tenancy: take them from configuration you own, never from the request. IN lists are the other common case: generate one placeholder per element from the count, and pass the elements as arguments.
sections.title: Identifiers and keywords need an allow-list, not a placeholder
sections.walkthrough: This fragment runs in your own service against a real PostgreSQL driver. The SQL text is built only from a number your code controls, so this concatenation is safe; every id still travels as an argument. The empty-list check matters because IN () is a syntax error, and the upper bound matters because every database limits how many parameters one statement may carry. Drivers that encode slices can bind a whole array instead, as in id = ANY($1) with PostgreSQL.

sections.body: Binding a search term stops injection into the statement, but LIKE interprets the bound value: % matches any run of characters and _ matches exactly one. A user searching for 100% or snake_case gets wrong results, and a pattern that begins with % cannot use an ordinary B-tree index, so a public search box needs length and rate limits anyway. Escape the wildcards and the escape character itself, then name that character in an ESCAPE clause instead of relying on a default: PostgreSQL and MySQL default to backslash, SQLite has none, and in MySQL a backslash inside a string literal is itself an escape, which is why the example uses !. Treat other embedded languages the same way: regular expressions, full-text query syntax and JSON path expressions accept operators inside a bound value, so validate their size and shape too.
sections.title: A bound LIKE pattern is still a small language

sections.body: Most real injections in Go services come through escape hatches. Query builders and ORMs offer raw-SQL methods for ORDER BY, WHERE fragments and JSON operators, and a fmt.Sprintf passed to one of them is exactly as dangerous as concatenating in db.QueryContext. Second-order injection is the delayed version: a value is stored safely through a parameter, then a reporting job or migration reads it back and splices it into dynamic SQL, trusting it because it came from your own database. Stored procedures that assemble EXECUTE strings move the problem into SQL instead of removing it. Some drivers can be configured to interpolate arguments on the client rather than using server-side parameters, which shifts escaping into the driver; keep the default unless you have measured a reason. Finally, limit the blast radius: the application's database role should not own the schema or read tables it never queries.

sections.body: In review, look at every QueryContext, ExecContext and QueryRowContext call and ask whether its query argument is a constant or is assembled only from fragments your code owns. Static analysis helps: gosec reports SQL built with string formatting or concatenation (rules G201 and G202). In tests, send hostile values such as quotes, semicolons, comment markers and wildcard characters through the real queries against a disposable database and assert on the rows returned, not merely on the absence of an error. A recording driver like the one above is useful in unit tests to assert that a function sends a constant statement and exactly the expected arguments.

In the first href it inspects the scheme, refuses javascript: and substitutes #ZgotmplZ, a deliberately meaningless marker. In the query string it percent-encodes the value, so & cannot start a new parameter. Inside <script> it emits a quoted JavaScript string with < and > written as \u003c and \u003e, so the browser never sees a tag. The Bio line is identical in both outputs because template.HTML told html/template the value is already safe markup.

sections.body: ZgotmplZ is the innocuous word html/template emits when an unsafe value reaches a URL, CSS or attribute-name position at run time. In URL attributes the filter passes relative references and the http, https and mailto schemes; javascript:, data: and every other scheme become #ZgotmplZ. Seeing it in rendered HTML means the data and the template disagree about what is allowed, so fix the data or the design instead of reaching for a conversion. html/template also refuses templates it cannot analyze: a template that ends inside an unclosed tag or attribute, an action in an ambiguous part of a URL, or if branches that leave the parser in different contexts make Execute return an error. Treat those errors as defects caught before any browser saw the page.

sections.body: html/template skips escaping for values of type template.HTML, HTMLAttr, URL, JS, JSStr, CSS and Srcset in their matching contexts. The conversion checks nothing; it is a claim, made by whoever wrote it, that the string is already safe there. That claim is correct for markup your own code generated, for the output of another executed template and for the output of a maintained HTML sanitizer. It is wrong for user input, for rows another service wrote, for Markdown rendered without sanitizing and for JSON pasted into a script as template.JS. Keep conversions rare, next to the code that produced the value and easy to search for, so a reviewer can list every place the escaper is switched off.

sections.body: html/template assumes the template text is trusted and only the data is not, so never parse a template from user input. Its guarantees end at the HTML it writes. A JSON API whose data the frontend inserts with innerHTML is DOM-based XSS, and the fix lives in that JavaScript. A handler that writes user bytes with w.Write or Gin's c.Data and a text/html content type bypasses templates entirely, and an uploaded file served from your origin needs a correct Content-Type plus X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, ideally from a separate download domain. In Gin, c.HTML renders through html/template, so templates loaded with LoadHTMLGlob get contextual escaping, while c.String responds as text/plain. A Content-Security-Policy, covered in the headers lesson, is the second layer for the day an escaping decision goes wrong.

A golden-file test per template is cheap and catches the regression a human reviewer is least likely to notice.

readings.introduction: Cross-site request forgery abuses ambient credentials. A page on another site submits a form or calls fetch toward your service, the browser attaches your session cookie, and your handler sees an authenticated request it never meant to accept. Since Go 1.25 the standard library ships http.CrossOriginProtection, which rejects non-safe cross-origin browser requests using the Sec-Fetch-Site and Origin headers instead of a per-form secret. This lesson shows what that check decides, where SameSite fits and what stays your responsibility.
readings.nuance: Only same-origin and none pass the Sec-Fetch-Site check; same-site and cross-site are rejected unless a trusted origin or a bypass pattern applies.
readings.objective: Protect cookie-authenticated endpoints with net/http's CrossOriginProtection, know what SameSite cookies add and recognize when a synchronizer token is still required.
readings.question: CrossOriginProtection receives a POST from blog.example.com to app.example.com with Sec-Fetch-Site: same-site. What happens?
readings.reviewAnswer: Rejected: a sibling subdomain is another origin

sections.body: A forged request is genuine HTTP from the victim's own browser, with the victim's cookie and network address, so authentication succeeds. What differs is the initiator: a document from another origin started it. Modern browsers say so. Sec-Fetch-Site carries same-origin, same-site, cross-site or none (the user typed the URL or opened a bookmark), and the Origin header names the initiating origin on POST and CORS requests. Page scripts cannot set either header. A server that refuses state-changing requests initiated by another origin removes the attack without storing anything per session. Credentials that are not ambient, such as a bearer token the client adds to an Authorization header, are never attached by the browser on its own, so they are not exposed to CSRF in the first place.
sections.title: The browser attaches the cookie; the server must ask who initiated

sections.body: The program wraps a ServeMux with http.NewCrossOriginProtection, trusts one partner origin, exempts a single-sign-on endpoint that receives a cross-site form post by design and replaces the default 403 body. Each probe sets the headers a particular client would send. httptest.NewRequest uses example.com as the Host, which is what the Origin fallback compares against.
sections.title: Wrap the mux and probe it with every kind of client
sections.walkthrough: GET, HEAD and OPTIONS pass unconditionally, which is why the cross-site GET succeeds: handlers behind those methods must never change state. A POST with Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin passes, and so would none; cross-site and same-site are both rejected, because a sibling subdomain is a different origin even though cookies treat it as the same site. Without Sec-Fetch-Site the check compares the Origin host with the Host header, and a request with neither header is treated as a non-browser client such as curl and passes. AddTrustedOrigin matches the full scheme://host[:port] string exactly. AddInsecureBypassPattern uses ServeMux pattern syntax, and a bypassed handler must authenticate the request another way; here the identity provider's signed assertion does that.

sections.body: SameSite=Lax tells the browser to omit the cookie on cross-site subrequests and cross-site POST navigations while still sending it on top-level GET navigations, so a user following a link arrives logged in. Strict withholds it on those navigations too. Both are worth setting on a session cookie, as the session lesson does, but neither replaces an origin check. Site is not origin: blog.example.com and app.example.com are the same site, so a compromised or user-generated subdomain still gets your cookies attached to its requests. Browsers also disagree about the default when SameSite is omitted, and Lax still sends the cookie on top-level GETs, which leaves any state-changing GET handler exposed. Use SameSite to shrink the attack surface and CrossOriginProtection to make the decision.
sections.title: SameSite cookies narrow exposure; they do not make the decision

sections.body: Wrap the outermost handler so a route added next quarter is protected automatically, and keep exemptions to a short, reviewed list. Because a *gin.Engine implements http.Handler, cop.Handler(router) protects every Gin route without Gin-specific middleware. If a reverse proxy rewrites the Host header, the Origin fallback for older browsers compares against the wrong host; preserve Host at the proxy or register the public origin with AddTrustedOrigin. Review CORS separately: it decides which origins may read responses, a different question from which may send writes, and a credentialed CORS policy that reflects any origin leaks GET responses even while writes are blocked.
sections.title: Put the check outside everything else
sections.walkthrough: This fragment runs in your own environment. AddTrustedOrigin returns an error for a value with a path, query or fragment, or without a scheme or host, so check it at startup. Call SetDenyHandler if clients expect a JSON error body; otherwise rejections get a plain-text 403. For a decision inside one handler, Check(r) returns the same error without writing a response.

sections.body: Header-based protection depends on the browser. CrossOriginProtection allows requests that carry neither Sec-Fetch-Site nor Origin, which covers API clients but also very old browsers that send neither on a form post. For a browser that sends Origin but not Sec-Fetch-Site it compares hosts only, so an http:// page on your own host looks like the https:// one; HSTS closes that gap. If policy requires protection for such clients, or if a state change must stay reachable through GET, add a synchronizer token: a random value bound to the session, embedded in each form and compared on submission. Tokens, usually together with re-authentication, also suit especially sensitive actions such as changing an account's email address. No CSRF defense survives XSS on your own origin, because injected script runs same-origin; that is the job of escaping and CSP.
sections.title: When a synchronizer token is still needed

sections.body: Test the protection as a table, as the program does: each kind of client, each method, trusted and untrusted origins, and every bypass pattern, asserting both the status and that the handler had no side effect. Review every GET handler for writes, because safe methods always pass. In an end-to-end browser test, submit a form from a second origin and expect a 403. Log rejections with method, path and Origin, so a legitimate integration broken by the check is visible within minutes instead of being reported as a vague 403 days later.
sections.title: Test the decision table

readings.takeaway: Wrap the whole handler in http.CrossOriginProtection, keep GET handlers free of side effects, set SameSite on session cookies as a second layer and add synchronizer tokens only where policy requires old-browser coverage.
readings.title: CSRF: reject cross-origin writes with Sec-Fetch-Site and http.CrossOriginProtection
wrongAnswers: Allowed, because SameSite cookies treat it as the same site
Allowed whenever an Origin header is also present

cautions: Max-Age and Expires are instructions to the browser, not enforcement.
An in-memory store is per-process and loses every session on restart.
designGuide.cost: A shared session store with TTLs and a user-to-session index, plus one lookup on every authenticated request.
strengths: The prefix and attributes are enforced by the browser on every request.
Server-side expiry and deletion work even when a cookie was copied.

readings.hint: Think about who else might already know the ID that existed before login.
readings.introduction: A session cookie is a bearer credential: whoever presents it is the user until the server decides otherwise. Its attributes control where the browser sends it and whether page scripts can read it; the server-side record controls how long it is honored. Getting either half wrong produces familiar incidents: a cookie copied out by an injected script, a session an attacker fixed before the victim logged in, or a logout that only deleted the browser's copy.
readings.nuance: Session fixation relies on the identifier surviving authentication. Rotating it, and deleting the old record, makes any copy obtained before login worthless.
readings.objective: Issue a __Host- session cookie with the right attributes, rotate the ID at login and enforce idle, absolute and logout expiry in a server-side store.
readings.question: Why must a login handler issue a new session ID instead of attaching the user to the current one?
readings.reviewAnswer: A pre-login ID an attacker planted becomes useless
readings.reviewPrompt: Why issue a new ID at login?

sections.body: HttpOnly hides the cookie from document.cookie, so an XSS payload cannot copy it out, although it can still send requests while the page is open. Secure stops the browser from sending it over plain HTTP. SameSite=Lax keeps it off cross-site subrequests and form posts, which narrows CSRF exposure. Path=/ with no Domain attribute makes a host-only cookie that is not sent to sibling subdomains. The __Host- name prefix turns those properties into browser-enforced rules: a cookie named __Host-session is rejected unless it is Secure, set from a secure origin, has Path=/ and carries no Domain, so a compromised subdomain cannot plant or overwrite it. Go's net/http does not check prefix rules; the browser does.
sections.title: What each attribute buys

sections.body: The program models a session store with an injected clock, so expiry is deterministic. The cookie carries only a random ID from crypto/rand.Text; the user, the creation time and the last activity live on the server. It walks through a login that follows a planted pre-login ID, idle expiry, absolute expiry of a busy session and logout, and prints the Set-Cookie headers with the random value masked.
sections.title: A store that owns expiry and rotation
sections.walkthrough: http.SetCookie renders the attributes in a fixed order; Max-Age=28800 matches the eight-hour absolute limit, but the server never relies on the browser forgetting the cookie. login destroys the old record before creating a new one, so the planted ID is dead and the user gets a fresh 26-character base32 ID; rand.Text guarantees at least 128 bits of randomness and may return longer strings in future releases. lookup checks the absolute limit against created and the idle limit against lastSeen, deletes expired records and refreshes lastSeen only on success. The busy session survives nineteen requests 25 minutes apart and still ends after eight hours. destroy removes the record, so a copied cookie replayed after logout finds nothing, and the final header, empty with Max-Age=0, asks the browser to drop its copy.

sections.body: Session fixation works when an application keeps the identifier it issued before login. An attacker obtains a valid anonymous ID, gets it into the victim's browser through a crafted link, a sibling subdomain or an injected header, and waits; once the victim authenticates, the attacker's copy of the same ID is logged in too. Issuing a new ID at login, and again whenever privileges rise, for example after step-up authentication or entering an admin mode, makes every earlier copy worthless. Carry over only the pre-login data you choose, such as a cart, by copying it into the new record. The __Host- prefix makes planting harder; rotation makes it pointless. Use both.
sections.title: Rotate the ID on every privilege change

sections.body: Gin's positional c.SetCookie(name, value, maxAge, path, domain, secure, httpOnly) takes SameSite from a separate c.SetSameSite call and URL-escapes the value, which makes a missing attribute easy to overlook; c.SetCookieData accepts a complete http.Cookie. Leave Domain empty: setting it to example.com widens the cookie to every subdomain and is forbidden with the __Host- prefix. Over plain HTTP on a development hostname the browser drops a Secure cookie, so run development over HTTPS rather than adding a flag that disables Secure and can leak into a release.
sections.title: Set and clear the cookie in net/http and Gin
sections.walkthrough: This fragment runs inside your own handler. MaxAge is in seconds, and a negative value emits Max-Age=0, which deletes the cookie. Both calls produce the same header, so a test can assert on the Set-Cookie string exactly as the program does. Gin's SetCookieData fills in Path and SameSite only when they are empty, so the explicit values above are what is sent.

sections.body: An idle timeout limits how long an abandoned, unlocked laptop stays logged in; an absolute timeout limits how long a stolen cookie is useful even if the thief keeps it busy. Choose both from the application's risk, for example 30 minutes idle and 8 hours absolute for an admin console, and enforce them where the record lives, not through Max-Age or Expires, which only instruct an honest browser. Logout must delete the server record and then clear the cookie; clearing only the cookie leaves every copied value valid. Plan the other invalidations too: a password change or account lock should end all of the user's sessions, which needs an index from user to session IDs. A real store is Redis or a database table with TTLs and that index; the in-memory map here is a model that loses everything on restart and is not shared between replicas.
sections.title: Expiry and logout belong to the server

sections.body: Read the Set-Cookie header in a test rather than the struct you meant to send, and assert HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite, Path=/ and the __Host- name. Assert that the ID changes across login and that the old ID fails afterwards. Advance a fake clock past the idle and the absolute limits and expect rejection, and replay a cookie after logout. Keep session IDs out of logs, URLs and analytics events. If a leaked session table would be serious, store a hash of each ID instead of the ID itself, a token-design decision covered elsewhere in this course.
sections.title: Review checklist

readings.takeaway: Name the cookie __Host-, set HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite and Path=/, issue a fresh crypto/rand ID at every login and enforce idle, absolute and logout expiry in the server-side store.
readings.title: Session cookies: lock down the attributes and keep the session's lifetime on the server
wrongAnswers: HttpOnly cookies cannot be updated after they are set
A new ID stops injected scripts from reading the cookie

cautions: Root does not stop mount points, device files or hard links inside the tree.
archive/zip accepts non-local entry names unless zipinsecurepath=0 is set.
designGuide.cost: Passing a *os.Root instead of a base-path string and a few checks per archive entry; component-wise resolution adds a little work to each open.
strengths: Neither .. nor symlinks can lead outside the opened directory.
Errors carry only the relative name, so they are safe to log.

readings.hint: Ask what Clean and Join know about the files that actually exist.
readings.introduction: Path traversal turns a file name from a request into access somewhere else on disk: ../ segments, an absolute path or a symlink that leads out of the intended directory. The classic Go defense, filepath.Join plus Clean plus a prefix check, works on strings while the kernel resolves the real path later, symlinks included. Go 1.24 added os.Root, which opens a directory once and resolves every later name inside it, and Go 1.25 extended it with ReadFile, WriteFile, MkdirAll and other helpers.
readings.nuance: Both functions are purely lexical. A symlink inside the directory can point anywhere, so only resolution relative to an open directory, as os.Root does, is a boundary.
readings.objective: Open user-named files through os.Root, use filepath.IsLocal and Localize for early rejection and extract archives without zip-slip.
readings.question: A handler joins a cleaned file name to its upload directory before opening it. Why can the opened file still be outside that directory?
readings.reviewAnswer: It edits strings; symlinks resolve later on disk

sections.body: filepath.Clean removes . and .. elements and duplicate separators, and filepath.Join cleans its result. Neither consults the disk. If the base directory contains a symbolic link, whether uploaded by a user, unpacked from an archive or left by a deploy, a clean, local-looking name such as latest.txt can resolve to a file outside the base. Prefix checks add their own bug: strings.HasPrefix(p, "/srv/public") also accepts /srv/public-backup. And code that resolves symlinks first and opens second can be raced by a concurrent rename. The robust design resolves the name relative to an already-open directory, one component at a time, and refuses any step that leaves it.
sections.title: Lexical checks cannot see the filesystem

sections.body: The program builds a small tree under os.TempDir(): a public directory with readme.txt, a secret.txt beside it and a relative symlink inside public that points at the secret. It asks for four names in three ways: the lexical filepath.IsLocal test, a naive Join of the cleaned name, and Root.ReadFile on a root opened at public. The deferred RemoveAll deletes the whole tree afterwards.
sections.title: Compare a string join with os.Root
sections.walkthrough: IsLocal rejects ../secret.txt and /readme.txt, but reports latest.txt as local because it never looks at the disk. The naive join leaks the secret twice: once through .., and once through the symlink that no lexical check can see. Join treats /readme.txt as relative, so that request happens to stay inside, which is luck rather than policy. os.Root refuses all three escapes with the same error, path escapes from parent. The error's path is the name you passed, never the root's location, so it is safe to log. Root follows symlinks only while they stay inside the root and rejects absolute link targets outright.

sections.body: Rejecting obviously bad names before touching the disk gives clear 400 responses and readable logs. filepath.IsLocal reports whether a path is non-empty, not absolute and still inside its base after lexical cleaning; on Windows it also rejects reserved names such as NUL. When names arrive slash-separated, as in URLs, io/fs paths and archives, filepath.Localize converts them to the OS form and fails for anything that is not a valid io/fs path, so its result is always local. Neither function sees symlinks, so pair them with os.Root. To serve a directory over HTTP, http.FileServerFS(root.FS()) keeps the confinement, whereas http.Dir and os.DirFS document that they follow symlinks wherever they point.
sections.title: IsLocal and Localize are early filters, not boundaries

sections.body: Zip-slip is path traversal delivered in bulk: an entry named ../../escape.txt or /etc/cron.d/job is written wherever it points if extraction code joins entry names to a destination. archive/zip still accepts such names by default in Go 1.27; only with GODEBUG=zipinsecurepath=0 does NewReader return ErrInsecurePath, alongside a usable reader. The extractor below validates each name with Localize, refuses symlinks and other non-regular entries, writes through os.Root with O_EXCL so it never follows or overwrites an existing file, and caps each file's size.
sections.title: Extract archives without zip-slip
sections.walkthrough: Directory entries are skipped because Root.MkdirAll creates parents on demand. Localize rejects the two hostile names before any write, and the symlink entry is refused by its mode rather than its name. Writes go through root.OpenFile, so even a name that passed every check cannot follow a link already present in the destination. io.LimitReader allows one byte past the limit so an oversize entry is detected rather than silently truncated. Running the program prints one wrote or skip line per entry and removes its temporary directory. Production extractors also cap the entry count and the total uncompressed size, because a small upload can expand into gigabytes.

sections.body: os.Root guarantees that names resolve beneath the root; it does not make everything beneath the root safe. It does not stop traversal across mount points or bind mounts inside the tree, it does not hide device files or /proc entries reachable within it, and a hard link inside the root to a file elsewhere is simply a file inside the root. On Unix, Root.Chmod, Chown and Chtimes have a documented race with symlink swaps. Prefer designs where users never name paths: store uploads under server-generated IDs, keep the original filename as metadata, and look files up by ID after an authorization check. In tests, keep a table of hostile names, including .., absolute paths, encoded dots if any layer decodes them and a planted symlink, and assert that every one is refused. Run the service as a user that cannot read secrets it does not need.
sections.title: What os.Root does not promise, and better designs

readings.takeaway: Reject non-local names early with filepath.IsLocal or Localize, then perform every file operation through os.Root so that .. and symlinks cannot leave the directory.
readings.title: Path traversal: confine file access with os.Root, because Join and Clean only edit strings
wrongAnswers: Clean keeps .. segments when the name is absolute
Join returns an error for .. that the handler ignores

cautions: -- is honored by each program's parser, not by Go; check the target tool.
A nil Env hands every secret in the service's environment to the child.
designGuide.cost: An allow-list per tool, explicit Env and Dir and a bounded output writer; starting a process stays far more expensive than calling a library.
strengths: Without a shell, no metacharacter in a user value is ever parsed.
cmd.Args can be asserted in tests without running anything.

readings.hint: Ask who reads argv once the new process has started.
readings.introduction: Go's os/exec does not invoke a shell: exec.Command takes a program and an argument slice, so semicolons and $(...) inside an argument are ordinary bytes. The operations lessons on Bash arguments and safe CLIs already rely on that. This lesson covers the injection that survives without a shell: a user value read as an option by the target program, an operation chosen by the request, and a child process that inherits your environment and outlives its deadline.
readings.nuance: Each program parses its own arguments, so a value starting with - can become a flag. -- ends option parsing in programs that support it, and validation covers those that do not.
readings.objective: Start external tools with exec.CommandContext and a fixed argv, block argument injection with validation and --, and bound the child's time and environment.
readings.question: exec.Command runs no shell. Why put "--" before a user-supplied file name in the argument list?
readings.reviewAnswer: The program parsing that value as an option
readings.reviewPrompt: What does -- before a value stop?

sections.body: Shell injection needs a shell: sh -c, bash -c, cmd /c, or a script that hands its arguments to eval. Concatenating a user value into that single command string lets ; | && and $( ) start new commands, and quoting by hand fails on the first input that contains a quote. Argument injection needs no shell at all. Every program parses its own argv, so a value beginning with a dash is read as an option: --files0-from=FILE for GNU wc, --upload-pack=COMMAND for git ls-remote, -o for many tools that write files. The exec call is correct and the user still controls the program's behavior. Defending against both means deciding which argv positions hold data and making the target program agree.
sections.title: Two injections: shell syntax and argument position

sections.body: The program constructs commands and prints cmd.Args, the exact argv the child would receive. It never calls Run, Start or Output, so no process starts. It contrasts a shell string with a direct argv, rejects names that begin with a dash, and builds git invocations from an allow-list of operations with a timeout, a controlled environment and a bounded wait.
sections.title: Build the argv and print it without running anything
sections.walkthrough: In the shell form the hostile name is part of one script, so sh would run touch pwned after wc. In the direct form the same bytes are one argument after --, and wc would only report that no file has that odd name. countLines rejects a leading dash before -- even matters; that also catches a lone -, which conventionally means standard input and which -- does not neutralize. gitCommand never copies request text into argv: the request selects a key, the argv comes from the map, and push is refused. Env replaces the environment entirely rather than adding to it. Cancel sends SIGTERM instead of the default Kill when the context ends (Windows supports only Kill), and WaitDelay bounds how long Wait then waits for the process to exit and its pipes to close. Args[0] is the name as written; the resolved executable is in cmd.Path.

sections.body: -- is a convention of each program's option parser, not of the kernel or of Go. Most getopt-style tools honor it, some treat it as data, and git uses it to separate revisions from paths, so git log -- main means the path main; git 2.24 and later accept --end-of-options for the revision case. Read the target's documentation, place user values after the terminator it actually supports, and still reject values that start with a dash when the field never legitimately does. Where the tool can read data from standard input or a file, prefer that over argv for free-form text. Never let a request choose the program name, and avoid wrapping tools whose purpose is to run other commands, such as find -exec, xargs, env, ssh or a script that calls eval.
sections.title: Make the target program agree where options end

sections.body: Map each user-visible operation to a complete argv in code, as gitOps does, and validate the few free-form values against strict patterns: a commit hash as 40 hexadecimal characters, a branch name against the repository's real branch list. Since Go 1.19, exec.LookPath refuses a program found through a relative PATH entry such as . and returns exec.ErrDot, which closes a classic hijack; an absolute path from configuration is clearer still. On Windows, a command line is a single string that each program parses itself, and .bat or .cmd files are interpreted by cmd.exe with its own metacharacters, so do not pass untrusted arguments to batch files there.
sections.title: Choose the executable and the operation in code

sections.body: A request-scoped context lets a client disconnect or a deadline stop the child. By default CommandContext kills the process when the context is done, but a grandchild holding the output pipes can still keep Wait blocked, which is what WaitDelay bounds. Set Env explicitly: a nil Env inherits every variable of your service, including database URLs and API tokens, which the child may log or forward. Set Dir rather than relying on the service's working directory, cap captured output, and return a generic error to the client while logging argv and exit status for operators.
sections.title: Bound time, output and inherited state
sections.walkthrough: This fragment runs in your own service and reuses gitCommand from the program. newLimitedBuffer stands for a small io.Writer you write that returns an error once its byte budget is spent; an unbounded bytes.Buffer lets a chatty tool exhaust memory. Checking ctx.Err() separates a timeout from a non-zero exit, so the client sees 504 for one and 500 for the other, and neither response includes the tool's stderr.

sections.body: Until Start is called, an exec.Cmd is a plain struct, so unit tests can assert on cmd.Args, cmd.Env and cmd.Dir for every operation and every hostile input, exactly as the program prints them, without installing the tool. Add a few integration tests that really run the command against a fixture directory with a short timeout. In review, search for sh -c, bash -c and cmd /c, for exec.Command calls whose program is not a constant, and for request-handling code that leaves Env nil.
sections.title: Test the argv, not the side effect

readings.takeaway: Pass a fixed program and argv to exec.CommandContext, take operations from an allow-list, keep user values out of option position with validation and the target's terminator, and set Env, Dir, Cancel and WaitDelay deliberately.
readings.title: Command injection: run tools without a shell and keep user input out of option position
wrongAnswers: It stops the shell from expanding ; and | characters
It makes os/exec quote the argument for the kernel

cautions: net/url and browsers disagree on backslashes, tabs and userinfo.
http.Redirect cleans relative paths but passes //host targets through.
designGuide.cost: A small validator and a host allow-list; keeping return paths server-side costs one session field.
strengths: Only two target shapes exist, so the policy fits in a short table.
Rejected input is never echoed into the Location header.

readings.hint: Compare how a browser resolves two leading slashes with how a file path would.
readings.introduction: Login, logout and OAuth flows often carry a next or return_to parameter. If the server redirects to whatever it contains, an attacker can send a link that starts on your trusted domain and ends on a lookalike login page, and in OAuth flows a redirect can leak codes or tokens. The obvious fix, allow only relative paths, is harder than it looks: browsers parse URLs by the WHATWG URL Standard, Go's net/url follows RFC 3986, and every difference between them is a bypass.
readings.nuance: Two leading slashes begin a scheme-relative URL: the browser keeps the current scheme and switches to the host after the slashes. Require exactly one leading slash.
readings.objective: Validate redirect targets so only same-site paths and allow-listed https URLs pass, including the //host, backslash and userinfo tricks that browsers and net/url read differently.
readings.question: A login handler redirects to next only if it starts with "/". Why is next=//evil.example still dangerous?
readings.reviewAnswer: No: browsers read // as the start of a new host

sections.body: A target of //evil.example/login starts with a slash, yet browsers read it as a scheme-relative URL that changes the host. Browsers also treat a backslash like a forward slash in http and https URLs, so /\evil.example becomes //evil.example on its way to the address bar, and they delete tab and newline characters anywhere in a URL, so a slash, a tab and another slash collapse into the same thing. Absolute URLs bring their own tricks: in https://docs.example.com@evil.example the first part is userinfo and the host is evil.example, and https://docs.example.com.evil.example/ passes any check that only compares a prefix. None of these needs a bug in your router, only validation that inspects a string instead of the destination a browser will compute.
sections.title: Why starting with / is not the same as staying on this site

sections.body: redirectTarget accepts exactly two shapes: a relative reference that begins with a single slash, or an https URL whose host is on an explicit allow-list. Everything else is rejected with a reason. The table compares it with a common first attempt that allows anything beginning with / or with the docs prefix, and the last two lines run the validator inside a login handler through httptest.
sections.title: A decision table for redirect targets
sections.walkthrough: Backslashes and control characters are rejected before parsing, because net/url either keeps them as path bytes or refuses them while a browser silently rewrites them. url.Parse then decides the shape: no scheme, no host and no userinfo means a relative reference, which must start with one slash and not two. For absolute URLs, u.Host, which includes any port, must equal an allow-list entry, so the userinfo and suffix tricks reveal their real hosts. https:evil.example parses with an empty host and an opaque part, and javascript: URLs have no host either, so both fail. The handler never echoes a rejected value: it falls back to / and answers 303 See Other so the browser follows with GET after the login POST.

sections.body: url.Parse is a parser, not a validator. It accepts almost any string: settings parses as a relative path, javascript:alert(1) as a scheme with an opaque part, and a leading space simply becomes part of the path. It lowercases the scheme but not the host, so normalize the host with strings.ToLower if DOCS.example.com should match. Never allow-list by string suffix, because badexample.com ends with example.com; if subdomains are allowed, require the host to equal example.com or end with .example.com. http.Redirect, and Gin's c.Redirect, which calls it, turn a relative target into an absolute path and clean it, but they pass //evil.example and /\evil.example through unchanged, so they are not validators either. Validate first and redirect to the value you validated.
sections.title: What url.Parse does and does not tell you

sections.body: The safest redirect parameter is not a URL. Store the intended destination server-side, for example in the session before sending the user to log in, and carry nothing or an opaque key in the query string. When a client must name a destination, let it choose from names that map to URLs in configuration. OAuth makes this mandatory for redirect_uri: the OAuth 2.0 security best current practice requires authorization servers to compare it with pre-registered values by exact string match, and your own post-login return path deserves the same standard. If linking to external sites is a product feature, show an interstitial page that displays the destination instead of redirecting silently.
sections.title: Better still: do not accept URLs at all

sections.body: Build the test table from transformations browsers actually apply: //host, backslashes, tabs and newlines inside the slashes or scheme, userinfo, suffix lookalikes, uppercase hosts, ports, the https:host form, javascript: and data: schemes, and percent-encoded slashes if any later component decodes them. Assert both the decision and the exact Location header. Run the same inputs through every place that redirects, including logout and error pages, because one unvalidated handler is enough. Log rejected values: repeated rejections are often the first visible sign that someone is testing phishing links against your login page.
sections.title: Test with a browser's eyes

readings.takeaway: Accept a redirect target only if it is a path starting with exactly one slash or an https URL whose exact host is allow-listed; reject backslashes and control characters first and fall back to a fixed page.
readings.title: Open redirects: accept a single-slash path or an allow-listed host, not any URL that parses
wrongAnswers: url.Parse rejects it, so the handler returns a 500
Browsers resolve it to /evil.example on the same host

cautions: HSTS includeSubDomains and preload are hard to undo; raise them deliberately.
Cached HTML that contains a nonce shares that nonce across visitors.
designGuide.cost: 16 random bytes and a few header writes per response, plus the one-time work of moving inline handlers into nonce-tagged scripts.
strengths: Injected scripts without the nonce do not run even if escaping fails.
One middleware gives every response the same baseline policy.

readings.hint: Think about what an attacker learns by viewing one of your pages.
readings.introduction: Response headers turn browser features into policy: which scripts may run, whether the page may be framed, whether a response may be reinterpreted as another content type, how much of the URL leaks to other sites and whether plain HTTP is ever acceptable again. None of them fixes a bug in your handlers. They limit what an escaping mistake, an injected script or a hostile frame can do, so they belong in one middleware that wraps every response.
readings.nuance: A nonce is a bearer value: anyone who knows it can tag their own script. A fresh random value per response cannot be learned in advance or replayed later.
readings.objective: Write middleware that sets a nonce-based Content-Security-Policy and the other baseline security headers, and roll them out without breaking pages or locking in HSTS preload by accident.
readings.question: Why must the CSP script nonce change on every response instead of being fixed per deployment?
readings.reviewAnswer: A reused nonce can be copied into injected scripts
readings.reviewPrompt: Why is a CSP nonce per response?

sections.body: Content-Security-Policy restricts where scripts, styles, frames and other resources may come from; with a strict script-src an injected <script> tag does not run. Strict-Transport-Security tells the browser to use HTTPS for this host for max-age seconds, so a network attacker cannot downgrade a later visit. X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff stops browsers from deciding that a text/plain or image response is really HTML or script. The frame-ancestors directive of CSP controls which origins may embed the page, which defeats clickjacking; X-Frame-Options: DENY is the legacy equivalent for old browsers, and a browser that enforces frame-ancestors ignores it when both are sent. Referrer-Policy limits how much of the current URL is sent in the Referer header. Leave out X-XSS-Protection: the filter it controlled is gone from modern browsers and could itself be abused.
sections.title: What each header defends against

sections.body: The middleware draws a 128-bit nonce from crypto/rand for every response, sets all headers before calling the next handler and stores the nonce in the request context. The handler renders it into the one script tag it trusts. To show what CSP adds, a bug elsewhere has marked a stored comment as template.HTML, so an injected script tag reaches the page. Two requests go through httptest, and the program prints the first response with the random nonce masked.
sections.title: Headers middleware with a per-request nonce
sections.walkthrough: script-src lists only the nonce, so a browser runs the script tag that carries it and refuses the injected one, which has no nonce and could not have guessed it; that is defense in depth on top of the escaping lesson, not a replacement. default-src 'self' covers other resource types, object-src 'none' disables plugins and base-uri 'none' stops an injected <base> tag from redirecting relative script URLs. The handler renders into a buffer first, so a template error becomes a clean 500 instead of half a page. The 16 random bytes become 22 base64url characters, which need no escaping inside an HTML attribute, and the second response gets a different value. Headers are set before next runs because header changes after WriteHeader are ignored.

sections.body: A nonce works only if an attacker cannot predict or reuse it, so generate one per response, never per process or per user, and do not let a CDN cache HTML that contains it, or every visitor shares one value. Static pages cannot carry a fresh nonce; allow their inline scripts by hash ('sha256-...') instead. Under this policy inline event handlers such as onclick and javascript: URLs are blocked, so move that code into nonce-tagged scripts. Introduce a new policy as Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only with a report-to or report-uri endpoint, read the violations for a release or two, then enforce it. Keep the policy string in one place in code, so a page that needs an exception gets a reviewed, narrow change instead of 'unsafe-inline'.
sections.title: CSP in practice: nonces, caching and a report-only rollout

sections.body: Browsers ignore Strict-Transport-Security on plain-HTTP responses, so sending it on every response is harmless; it takes effect after the first HTTPS visit. Start with a short max-age such as 300 seconds, raise it to a year once every page and API works over HTTPS, and add includeSubDomains only when every subdomain, including internal tools and forgotten marketing hosts, serves valid HTTPS. The preload directive asks browser vendors to ship your domain in a built-in HTTPS-only list. Removal takes months to reach users, and meanwhile any subdomain without a working certificate is unreachable for everyone, so preload is a deliberate, owner-approved step, never a default in shared middleware. If TLS terminates at a load balancer, set HSTS there or here, but in exactly one place.
sections.title: HSTS: start short, preload last

sections.body: In Gin the policy is a middleware registered with r.Use before any route. c.Header sets a response header, c.Set stores the nonce for handlers and c.HTML renders through html/template, which escapes the nonce attribute like any other value. Register it on the engine rather than on a route group so that 404 and recovery responses carry the headers too, then assert them in a router test.
sections.title: The same middleware in Gin
sections.walkthrough: This fragment runs in your own Gin service and reuses newNonce from the program. c.Next runs the rest of the chain after the headers are set, so a handler can still override one header for one route, which is where a reviewed exception belongs. Gin builds its 404 chain from the engine's global middleware, so unmatched routes get these headers as well.

sections.body: Test headers as the program does: send requests through the full handler chain with httptest and compare each header with an exact expected string, masking only the nonce. Include an error page, a redirect, a static file and a 404, since those responses most often bypass middleware. Check that two responses never share a nonce and that the nonce in the header equals the one in the page. For pages whose URLs carry secrets, such as password-reset links, send Referrer-Policy: no-referrer on that response. In review, treat any new 'unsafe-inline', 'unsafe-eval', wildcard source or HSTS preload as a security change that needs its own justification.
sections.title: Test and review the headers

readings.takeaway: Set CSP with a fresh per-response nonce, nosniff, frame-ancestors plus X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy and a gradually raised HSTS in one outer middleware, and treat preload as a separate, deliberate decision.
readings.title: Security headers: a per-request CSP nonce, HSTS, nosniff, frame-ancestors and Referrer-Policy
wrongAnswers: Browsers reject a nonce they have already seen
The nonce is a hash of the script body it allows

cautions: Unexported fields bypass fmt methods, and encoding/json skips them silently.
Redacted hides only the userinfo password, not tokens in the query string.
designGuide.cost: A small wrapper type, a Reveal call at each use site and one canary test per output channel. It does not protect memory, core dumps or values already copied into plain strings.
strengths: Careless log lines and %+v dumps print a placeholder instead of the value.
Every intentional use is a searchable Reveal call.

readings.hint: fmt reaches field values through reflection; consider which values reflection may call methods on.
readings.introduction: Most leaked credentials are not stolen from a vault; they are printed. A startup line that logs the configuration with %+v, an error that wraps a connection string, a debug endpoint that dumps settings: each copies the secret into log storage that more people can read, for longer, than the secret store itself. Make printing safe by default and make revealing the value an explicit, searchable call.
readings.nuance: fmt cannot invoke Format, String or Error on unexported fields, so it prints their contents directly; encoding/json, by contrast, skips such fields entirely.
readings.objective: Wrap credentials in a Secret type that redacts itself in fmt, slog and JSON, redact credentials in URLs, and load secrets with errors that name the source but never the value.
readings.question: A Secret type implements Format and String, but another struct holds it in an unexported field. What does %+v print for that struct?
readings.reviewAnswer: fmt skips its methods and prints the raw value

sections.body: Trace a database password through a typical service. It is read from the environment into a Config struct; the struct is logged at startup so operators can see what was loaded; the password is placed in a connection URL; and when the database is down, the URL appears in a wrapped error that is logged on every retry. None of these steps looks like a leak in review. The log pipeline then ships each line to an aggregator, to backups and perhaps to a vendor, where access rules and retention are looser than in your secret store. Once the value is there, the only safe response is rotation. Prevention works best at the type level: if the value cannot print itself, the careless log line stays harmless.
sections.title: Follow a password from config to log line

sections.body: Secret keeps its value in an unexported field and implements four interfaces, because different encoders take different paths. fmt.Formatter covers every fmt verb, including %x and %q, and takes precedence over String and GoString. slog.LogValuer is resolved by slog handlers when a Secret is an attribute value. json.Marshaler covers JSON log handlers and API responses that embed the struct. String remains for code that asks for a fmt.Stringer directly. The program pushes a fake canary value through each path and checks whether it survived.
sections.title: A Secret type that redacts every formatting path
sections.walkthrough: A plain string field prints verbatim under %+v. Config.DBPassword is an exported field, so fmt calls Secret.Format on it and every verb prints [REDACTED]. The hidden struct shows the trap: fmt cannot invoke methods on unexported fields, so it falls back to reflection and prints {token:{value:canary-7f3a}}. The JSON handler resolves db_password through LogValue and encodes the nested config with json.Marshal, which calls MarshalJSON; the text handler formats the nested struct with %+v, which reaches Format. url.URL.String includes the password, while Redacted replaces it with xxxxx before the URL enters an error string. The final line confirms the canary never reached the log buffer.

sections.body: The type protects only the paths it implements, so learn the rules that bypass it. fmt and encoding/json both ignore methods on unexported struct fields: fmt prints the raw contents and json silently skips the field. slog resolves LogValuer on attribute values and inside groups, not inside struct fields, so a nested Secret relies on MarshalJSON in a JSON handler and on Format in a text handler. Calling Reveal hands out a plain string that no longer protects itself, so do it at the last moment, inside the call that needs it, such as building a driver configuration. Reflection-based dumpers and some third-party loggers walk struct fields directly; check how each one you use prints a value. If configuration is decoded from a file, give Secret an UnmarshalText method so it never exists as a plain string field. Keep the method name distinctive, so a search for Reveal lists every intentional use.
sections.title: Know which path each encoder takes

sections.body: Connection strings carry credentials in the userinfo part, and url.URL.String prints them. Redacted replaces only the password; it does not touch tokens in the query string, so keep API keys in headers, because proxies and access logs record URLs. The net/http client already replaces the password with *** in the *url.Error it returns, but errors you build with fmt.Errorf get no such help. When loading, accept either NAME or NAME_FILE, the convention for secrets that container platforms mount as files; reject both being set, trim the trailing newline that editors add, and refuse empty values. Every error names the variable or the file, never the content.
sections.title: Redact URLs and fail loudly without the value
sections.walkthrough: This second program compiles as shown; run it in your own environment. It writes a test secret under os.TempDir with mode 0600 and points ORDERS_DB_PASSWORD_FILE at it. The first line prints [REDACTED] <nil> true: the loaded Secret hides itself while Reveal still returns the canary. Setting both forms is ambiguous and fails; a missing variable fails with a message that tells the operator exactly what to provide; an empty value is treated as an error rather than silently connecting without a password. Call loadSecret during startup so a bad deployment fails before it accepts traffic.

sections.body: Environment variables are convenient but broad: every child process inherits them, Linux exposes them through /proc to the same user and to root, crash reporters often capture them, and os.Unsetenv after reading does not erase copies a supervisor already holds. Mounted files can carry tight permissions, can be rotated by replacing the file, and keep the value out of the environment. A secret manager adds audit trails, short-lived credentials and automatic rotation, at the cost of a network dependency during startup. Whatever the source, load secrets once at startup into Secret values, re-read files on a signal or timer if rotation must not need a restart, and never log a prefix of the value: a few characters of a short password narrow guessing considerably. To correlate rotations, log a key ID or version number, which is not secret.
sections.title: Choose where secrets live

sections.body: Add one test per output channel: build the real Config from a canary value, run the code that logs it at startup, render the error your connection code produces, encode the debug endpoint's JSON, and fail if the canary appears anywhere. The test is cheap and catches the regression that matters most, a new credential field added as a plain string. Keep a log-pipeline scrubber for known token formats as a second line of defense, but treat it as a backstop: by the time it runs, the secret has already left the process.
sections.title: Prove it with a canary test
sections.walkthrough: This _test.go fragment belongs in your service's package and runs with go test in your own environment; it also needs the bytes, log/slog, strings and testing imports. logStartup stands for whatever function production calls at boot. Testing that function rather than a copy of it is what makes the test meaningful. Printing the buffer on failure is safe here because the canary is not a real credential.

readings.takeaway: Wrap credentials in a type whose every formatting path prints a placeholder, keep secret fields exported or explicitly encoded, redact URLs before they reach errors, and fail at startup with messages that name the source, never the value.
readings.title: Keep secrets out of logs and errors with a type that refuses to print itself
wrongAnswers: [REDACTED], because Format is always called first
Nothing, because unexported fields are omitted

cautions: ConstantTimeCompare returns immediately when lengths differ.
Lookups, error messages and metrics around the comparison can still leak.
designGuide.cost: One hash and a full-length comparison per check, negligible next to a network round trip. The real cost is reviewing the surrounding path, which tests cannot do for you.
strengths: Removes the per-byte oracle that makes long tokens guessable.
Digest comparison also hides the length and lets you store only hashes.

readings.hint: Think about what happens to the response time as more of the guess is correct.
readings.introduction: A comparison that stops at the first differing byte takes longer the more of the guess is correct. Against a token, an API key or a MAC tag, that turns an impossible search over the whole value into a byte-by-byte search an attacker can run with enough repeated requests. Constant time here means time that depends only on public facts, such as the length, and never on the contents of the secret.
readings.nuance: The result is correct; the leak is in the duration. Work that grows with the matching prefix lets an attacker recover the token one byte at a time.
readings.objective: Recognize timing-dependent comparisons and replace them with crypto/subtle or hmac.Equal over fixed-size digests, including the lookup and error paths around them.
readings.question: Comparing a presented API token with == returns the right answer. Why is it still a vulnerability?
readings.reviewAnswer: It stops early, so timing reveals the correct prefix

sections.body: To guess a 20-byte token blindly, an attacker faces 256^20 candidates. If the server's comparison returns as soon as one byte differs, each response time hints at how many leading bytes were right. The attacker then fixes one position at a time: at most 256 candidates per byte across 20 bytes, a few thousand guesses, each repeated enough times to average out network noise. The difference per byte is tiny, but repeated measurements from a nearby network position, such as another tenant in the same cloud region, can resolve it. Go's == on strings and bytes.Equal make no timing promise and do stop early, so they are the wrong tool for secrets even though they are the right tool for everything else.
sections.title: Why an early return is an oracle

sections.body: Timing is noisy in a demo, so the program counts the bytes a naive loop examines, which is what its running time tracks. It then shows the standard tools: subtle.ConstantTimeCompare for equal-length values, a SHA-256 digest step that removes the length signal, and hmac.Equal for MAC tags computed with a test-only key.
sections.title: Measure the work instead of the nanoseconds
sections.walkthrough: The naive loop examines 1, 5, 11 and 20 bytes: its work grows with the correct prefix, and that growth is the oracle. subtle.ConstantTimeCompare XORs every byte pair and ORs the results, so for equal lengths its work does not depend on content; it returns the int 1 or 0, not a bool. The short guess returns 0 immediately, because the documented guarantee covers contents, not length. tokenMatches hashes the presented value first, so every comparison runs over two 32-byte digests whatever the caller sends. hmac.Equal is ConstantTimeCompare(...) == 1; the truncated tag fails because its length differs.

sections.body: ConstantTimeCompare returns at once when lengths differ, and its documentation says so. For tokens you issue in a fixed format, the length is public anyway. For values whose length is secret or chosen by someone else, such as a shared webhook secret or a legacy API key, compare digests: SHA-256 of either side is always 32 bytes. Hashing also lets you store only the digest, so a database read does not hand out working credentials; the token-design lesson builds on that. A fast hash is enough only for high-entropy values. Passwords need the slow, salted hashing of the password-storage lesson, because a fast digest of a guessable value is itself guessable. For MAC tags, compute the expected tag over the received message and compare the full length: code that compares only as many bytes as the client sent accepts a one-byte tag after at most 256 tries.
sections.title: Fixed-size digests close the length channel

sections.body: A constant-time compare inside a variable-time path still leaks. Look at the code around it: a lookup that returns early when a key ID is unknown, a database query with the secret in its WHERE clause, different messages or status codes for no such key and wrong key, and metrics labeled by failure reason all reveal information. Look credentials up by a public identifier or by the digest of the secret, compare in constant time, and return one generic error. When the identifier is unknown, compare against a dummy digest so both paths do the same work.
sections.title: The comparison is not the only branch
sections.walkthrough: This fragment shows the shape of an API key check; KeyStore, Principal and errUnauthorized belong to your service, and it runs in your own environment. The map lookup by a public key ID may take variable time because the ID is not secret. Both branches hash and compare, and the found check comes after the comparison, so an unknown ID and a wrong secret are indistinguishable in both result and work.

sections.body: Unit tests cannot prove constant time, and a benchmark that shows equal averages on a laptop says little about a loaded production CPU. Treat it as a review rule instead: every comparison of a token, MAC, API key, signature or password hash uses subtle.ConstantTimeCompare, hmac.Equal or a library verifier that does, over fixed-length inputs, followed by a single error path. Search for == and bytes.Equal near names such as token, secret, signature and digest. On arm64, subtle.WithDataIndependentTiming (Go 1.24) enables the processor's data-independent-timing mode for code that is already written in constant time; it does not repair variable-time code, and most services do not need it. Rate limiting the endpoint helps as well, because the attack needs many requests.
sections.title: Review it; do not try to benchmark it

readings.takeaway: Compare secrets with crypto/subtle or hmac.Equal over fixed-size digests, look them up by a public ID or by their hash, and give every failure the same error and the same amount of work.
readings.title: Compare secrets in constant time: an early return reveals how much of a guess was right
wrongAnswers: It compares string pointers, like == on Java strings
It is slow enough to enable a denial of service

cautions: A repeated nonce under one key breaks both confidentiality and integrity.
Ciphertext length reveals plaintext length, and encrypted columns are not searchable.
designGuide.cost: 33 bytes per record, one AES-GCM operation per read and write, and a re-encryption job plus a key inventory for every rotation.
strengths: Tampering, row swaps and wrong keys all fail with one authentication error.
Key IDs turn rotation into a gradual migration instead of a flag day.

readings.hint: Ask which input to Open the attacker cannot change by copying bytes between rows.
readings.introduction: Encrypting a column protects data in backups, replicas and database dumps, but only if the record format answers more than which key to use. The crypto-purposes lesson explains why encryption must be authenticated. This lesson builds the record envelope: AES-GCM through crypto/cipher, a fresh random nonce per seal, a key ID that survives rotation, and additional data that ties each ciphertext to the row it belongs to.
readings.nuance: The tag covers the additional data, so opening with the victim's record ID fails authentication even though the copied ciphertext itself is intact.
readings.objective: Seal application records with AES-GCM so that tampering, row swapping and key rotation are handled explicitly, and explain why a repeated nonce breaks GCM.
readings.question: An attacker with database write access copies their own encrypted bank details into a victim's row. What stops the application from accepting them?
readings.reviewAnswer: A ciphertext then opens only in the row it was sealed for
readings.reviewPrompt: Why pass the record ID as AD?

sections.body: Picture customers' bank details stored encrypted in a table, and three attackers. One reads a backup and should learn nothing but lengths. One flips bits in a ciphertext, hoping to change a value without knowing it. One can write to the database, perhaps through a bug elsewhere, and copies the ciphertext from their own row into a victim's row, so that the victim's next payout goes to the attacker's account. AES-GCM, an AEAD, handles the first two: it hides the plaintext, and its tag check rejects any modification. The third needs context. Passing the record ID as additional data, which is authenticated but not encrypted, means a ciphertext opens only in the row it was sealed for.
sections.title: What a record envelope must guarantee

sections.body: The envelope is version(1) || keyID(4) || nonce(12) || ciphertext || tag(16). cipher.NewGCMWithRandomNonce, added in Go 1.24, draws the nonce from crypto/rand and prepends it, so the caller cannot pass a stale one. The header and the record ID together form the additional data. The program prints sizes, booleans and errors rather than ciphertext, so its output is identical on every run even though keys and nonces are random.
sections.title: Seal, open, rotate and fail
sections.walkthrough: The 33-byte plaintext becomes 66 bytes: 5 of header, 12 of nonce and 16 of tag. Two seals of the same value differ because each draws a new nonce. Opening under customer-99 fails with cipher: message authentication failed, the same error as a flipped bit; GCM cannot say which part was wrong, and should not. additionalData clones the header before appending, so the append cannot write into the buffer Seal is about to fill. After key 2 is added, new records carry key ID 2 while the old record still opens with key 1, and deleting key 1 too early makes it unreadable. The final block is a labeled test path: cipher.NewGCM with a fixed all-zero nonce. Two messages sealed under one nonce let anyone who knows the first recover the second with XOR.

sections.body: GCM is counter mode plus a polynomial MAC. Reusing a nonce under the same key reuses the keystream, so the XOR of two ciphertexts equals the XOR of their plaintexts, as the test path shows. Worse, two messages under one nonce let an attacker solve for the authentication subkey and forge valid tags for messages of their choosing. A random 96-bit nonce keeps collisions negligible only within a budget: the NewGCMWithRandomNonce documentation says a key must not encrypt more than 2^32 messages. Counters avoid randomness but are hard to keep unique across replicas, restarts and restored backups. For very high volumes per key, rotate by message count or time, derive separate keys per tenant, or use XChaCha20-Poly1305 from golang.org/x/crypto/chacha20poly1305, whose 192-bit nonces can be chosen at random for far more messages.
sections.title: Nonces must never repeat under one key

sections.body: A key ID in every record is what makes rotation possible: readers choose the key from the record and writers always use the current key. Rotation then has three phases. Add the new key everywhere and make it current. Re-encrypt old rows in a background job that opens and reseals each one. Retire the old key only when a count of rows by key ID reaches zero; retiring first, as the program shows, turns rotation into data loss. In production the keys usually come from a key management service through envelope encryption: a master key held by the service encrypts the data keys your application uses, so rotating the master key re-wraps a few small data keys instead of rewriting every row. The key ID is not secret, but it is authenticated through the additional data, so editing it in place fails the tag check.
sections.title: Rotation is a data migration, not a config change

sections.body: An AEAD hides content, not size: here the ciphertext is always 33 bytes longer than the plaintext, so pad values whose length is sensitive. Encrypted columns cannot be searched or indexed; if you need equality lookups, store a separate HMAC of the normalized value under a different key, accepting that it reveals which rows are equal. Additional data must be unambiguous: when it combines several variable-length fields, length-prefix each one so that (ab, c) and (a, bc) differ. On an authentication failure, return an error and raise an alert; never log ciphertext next to plaintext, and never fall back to returning unauthenticated bytes. Tests should flip every byte of a sealed record, move it to another ID, open it after rotation and after retirement, and assert that a configured key is exactly 32 bytes.
sections.title: Limits and the review checklist

readings.takeaway: Use an AEAD with a fresh random nonce per seal, authenticate a versioned header and the record ID as additional data, carry a key ID for rotation, and retire a key only after no record uses it.
readings.title: Encrypt records with AES-GCM: random nonces, a key ID, and the record ID as additional data
wrongAnswers: A random nonce makes every ciphertext unique
AES-256 keys are too long to brute-force

cautions: Memory cost times concurrency can exhaust a server unless it is bounded.
bcrypt compares only the first 72 bytes of a password.
designGuide.cost: Tens of milliseconds of CPU and tens of MiB of memory per login by design, plus a semaphore, a rate limiter and a lazy migration path to maintain.
strengths: Parameters travel with each hash, so the policy can rise without resets.
Uniform errors and uniform work hide which accounts exist.

readings.hint: Upgrading needs an input that the database deliberately does not keep.
readings.introduction: The crypto-purposes lesson establishes that passwords need a slow, salted, memory-hard function. The operational questions come next: how to store the parameters with each hash so they can change later, how to upgrade old hashes without forcing resets, how to budget memory when many users log in at once, and how to keep the login endpoint from telling an attacker which accounts exist.
readings.nuance: A password hash cannot be reversed, so only a login that has just verified the password holds the plaintext needed to hash it again with new parameters.
readings.objective: Hash passwords with argon2id in a self-describing PHC-style string, upgrade parameters at login, handle bcrypt's 72-byte limit and keep login failures indistinguishable.
readings.question: Your argon2id policy raised the memory cost. How do existing accounts get the stronger hash without a forced reset?
readings.reviewAnswer: At a successful login, when the plaintext is available
readings.reviewPrompt: When can an old hash be upgraded?

sections.body: Assume an attacker eventually holds the users table. They can then guess offline as fast as their hardware allows, with no rate limit. A random per-user salt stops them from attacking every account at once with precomputed tables, and argon2id's memory cost makes each guess expensive on GPUs and custom hardware, not just on CPUs. Your parameters will need to rise as hardware improves, so every stored hash must record the algorithm, version and costs that produced it. The PHC string format does that in one column, for example $argon2id$v=19$m=19456,t=2,p=1$salt$hash, with salt and hash in unpadded standard base64.
sections.title: Design for the day the table leaks

sections.body: The program uses deliberately small costs so it finishes in milliseconds. It registers an account under an old policy, rejects an unknown email and a wrong password with the same error, upgrades the stored hash on a successful login, refuses a stored row with hostile parameters, and then shows bcrypt's length limit.
sections.title: Hash, verify and upgrade in one login path
sections.walkthrough: hash draws a 16-byte salt from crypto/rand and encodes the costs next to the result; params prints only the parameter prefix, because salt and hash change on every run. parse checks every field and bounds the costs, because a stored row is input too: m=4194304 would demand 4 GiB per login. verify recomputes with the stored parameters and compares with subtle.ConstantTimeCompare. login spends a full hash on unknown emails, returns one error for every failure, and rehashes when the policy has changed, the only moment the plaintext is available. bcrypt.GenerateFromPassword rejects a 73-byte password, yet CompareHashAndPassword silently uses only the first 72 bytes, so any suffix matches.

sections.body: The demo's 8 MiB and two passes are far too cheap. The OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet gives argon2id with m=19456 KiB (19 MiB), t=2 and p=1 as a minimum, with equivalent trade-offs such as m=47104 KiB and t=1. RFC 9106 recommends t=1 with 2 GiB, or t=3 with 64 MiB when memory is tighter, both with four lanes. Benchmark on production hardware and aim for a verification of tens of milliseconds, then multiply the memory by the concurrency you allow: fifty simultaneous logins at 64 MiB need more than 3 GiB. Bound concurrent hashing with a semaphore so a burst of login attempts produces fast errors instead of an out-of-memory crash. For existing bcrypt systems, OWASP recommends a cost of at least 10.
sections.title: Production parameters and a memory budget
sections.walkthrough: This fragment wraps the verify function from the program and runs in your own service. The buffered channel is a counting semaphore: a login takes a slot before hashing and returns it afterwards. When every slot is busy, the request waits until its context deadline, so overload produces quick, visible errors rather than unbounded memory growth. Size the slot count as the memory you can spare divided by the m parameter.

sections.body: Because parameters live in the hash, upgrading is lazy: when verification succeeds and the stored parameters differ from the current policy, hash the password again and save it. Accounts that never log in keep old hashes; to retire a weak scheme completely, require a reset for them after a deadline. The same dispatch migrates algorithms: a stored value that begins with $2a$ or $2b$ is bcrypt, so verify it with bcrypt and store an argon2id hash on success. bcrypt reads at most 72 bytes, and UTF-8 passphrases reach that sooner than their character count suggests. Since the x/crypto implementation refuses long passwords when hashing but not when comparing, cap password length at registration in bytes and remember that a longer password typed at login is checked on its first 72 bytes only. Moving to argon2id is simpler than pre-hashing passwords for bcrypt.
sections.title: Upgrade old hashes, including bcrypt

sections.body: A login endpoint leaks through its differences. Return the same message and status for an unknown email, a wrong password and a malformed stored hash, and spend the same work on each: the program hashes the submitted password even when no account exists, because skipping the hash makes unknown emails answer measurably faster. Registration and password-reset flows can reveal the same fact, so give them neutral responses such as: if the address exists, we sent a link. Hashing slows offline guessing only; online guessing needs throttling. Limit attempts per account and per source address, for example with golang.org/x/time/rate limiters held in a bounded cache, and prefer growing delays to hard lockouts that let anyone lock a victim out.
