Log failures with the account ID, never the submitted password, and test that every failure returns identical bodies and that rehashing happens exactly once.
sections.title: One answer for every failure, and fewer guesses

readings.takeaway: Store argon2id hashes with their parameters, bound the costs when parsing and the memory when verifying, rehash on a successful login when the policy changes, and make every login failure look and cost the same.
readings.title: Store passwords with argon2id: encoded parameters, rehash on login, one answer for every failure
wrongAnswers: Decrypt each stored hash and hash it again
Old hashes verify under the new parameters anyway

cautions: Signed tokens stay valid until exp unless verifiers check a deny-list.
HMAC verifiers share the signing key and can therefore mint tokens.
designGuide.cost: A lookup per request for opaque tokens, or key distribution, short lifetimes and a refresh flow for signed ones; either way, a table of hostile test tokens to maintain.
strengths: Hashed opaque tokens are useless from a leaked table and revoke instantly.
A strict verifier rejects whole families of attacks by construction.

readings.hint: Consider who wrote the header and what they would choose.
readings.introduction: The identity-authorization lesson says to validate a token's full contract before trusting the principal it names. This lesson designs the tokens themselves. Opaque tokens are random strings that mean nothing without a lookup, so revocation is immediate. Signed tokens carry their claims and verify without a lookup, so revocation is hard and every claim check is your job. Both need expiry, rotation and a plan for theft.
readings.nuance: The header is attacker-controlled input. Honoring it enables alg none and key-confusion attacks, so the expected algorithm must come from configuration bound to the key.
readings.objective: Choose between opaque and signed tokens, store opaque tokens as hashes with rotation and reuse detection, and verify HMAC-signed JWTs with a pinned algorithm and checked claims.
readings.question: A verifier reads alg from the token header and uses it to decide how to check the signature. What is wrong with that?
readings.reviewAnswer: The verifier's configuration, never the token header

sections.body: If the service that issues a token is the only one that checks it, as with browser sessions or first-party API keys, use an opaque token: 32 random bytes, encoded, with all state kept on the server. Revocation is a row update, and the token reveals nothing about the user if it leaks into a log. Signed tokens such as JWTs earn their complexity when many services must verify independently without calling the issuer. The price is that a stolen signed token stays valid until it expires, unless every verifier also consults a revocation list, which brings the lookup back. Keep signed access tokens short-lived, minutes rather than days, and pair them with an opaque refresh token that the issuer can revoke.
sections.title: Pick the token by who verifies it

sections.body: The store keeps only SHA-256 digests and is keyed by them, so a leaked table cannot be replayed and the lookup never compares the secret itself, as the constant-time lesson recommends. Refresh tokens rotate: each use returns a new token and marks the old one used. A second use of the same token means two parties hold it, so the whole family descending from that login is revoked. The clock is an injected function, which keeps expiry deterministic.
sections.title: Opaque tokens: store the digest, rotate on use
sections.walkthrough: issue draws 32 bytes from crypto/rand and adds a gfr_ prefix, giving 47 characters; a recognizable prefix lets secret scanners and log scrubbers find leaked tokens. lookup rejects the wrong shape before hashing, then checks family revocation and expiry against the injected clock. A one-character change misses the map entirely. Rotate returns a new token; replaying the original afterwards triggers reuse detection, which also invalidates the legitimate client's new token and forces a fresh login, a deliberate trade of convenience for containing theft. Moving the fixed clock forward 61 minutes expires the one-hour token.

sections.body: When you must verify JWTs, prefer a maintained library and configure it strictly. The program shows what strict means using only the standard library: the algorithm is pinned by configuration, the header may contain only alg, typ and kid, the signature is checked over the exact received bytes before any claim is parsed, and exp is mandatory. It runs ten tokens, from valid to hostile, against a fixed clock and a test-only key.
sections.title: A strict verifier for HMAC-signed tokens
sections.walkthrough: This second program compiles as shown; run it in your own environment and it prints one accepted line followed by nine rejections. alg none and HS512 fail the pinned algorithm before any key is chosen, which is the defense against algorithm switching: the token never selects how it is verified. decodeStrict rejects the jku header, closing the family of attacks that inject keys or key URLs. The edited payload keeps the original signature and fails hmac.Equal. exp 31 seconds in the past exceeds the 30-second leeway; nbf two minutes ahead fails; an audience list without orders-api fails; and a token without exp is refused instead of treated as eternal. base64URLOnly matters because Go's base64 decoders ignore newlines even in Strict mode.

sections.body: Give every token an absolute expiry and, for sessions, an idle timeout as well. Design revocation in from the start: for opaque tokens, delete or flag the record and revoke every family a user owns when the password changes; for signed tokens, keep lifetimes short or keep a deny-list of token IDs (jti) until their exp passes. Signing keys rotate through kid: publish the new key to verifiers first, start signing with it, and remove the old key only after the longest token lifetime has elapsed. Allow a clock-skew leeway of seconds, not hours. Use explicit typ values, such as at+jwt from RFC 9068 for access tokens, so an ID token or refresh token cannot be replayed where an access token is expected. Asymmetric algorithms such as EdDSA or ES256 let verifiers hold only public keys; with HMAC, every verifier can also mint tokens.
sections.title: Expiry, revocation and key rotation in production

sections.body: Keep the ten cases from the verifier as table tests and add those a library might mishandle: alg in a different case, a kid that names a key meant for another purpose, an aud claim that is a number, exp as a float or a string, very long tokens, and a valid token presented to a different service. Go's encoding/json matches field names case-insensitively and keeps the last of duplicate keys, so another parser in your system might read a different exp or sub than you do; reject such payloads or make sure only one parser ever interprets the token. For opaque tokens, test expiry at the exact boundary, reuse detection, revocation after a password change, and that no code path stores or logs the raw token.
sections.title: Hostile tokens for the test suite

readings.takeaway: Prefer hashed opaque tokens when the issuer is the verifier; when tokens must be signed, pin the algorithm, verify the exact bytes before parsing, require exp, and check iss, aud and nbf against an injected clock.
readings.title: Design tokens deliberately: hashed opaque tokens, strictly verified signed tokens, expiry and rotation
wrongAnswers: Nothing, as long as the signature check itself is correct
Only alg none is dangerous; other values are safe

cautions: Invariants define what fuzzing can find; a target that only parses finds only panics.
A limit on compressed size does not limit decompressed size.
designGuide.cost: A fuzz test per parser, CPU time for scheduled fuzzing runs and committed corpus files; the hardening itself costs a few comparisons per field.
strengths: Finds inputs you did not think of, often within seconds for small formats.
Saved failures become permanent regression tests that run with go test.

readings.hint: Two different byte strings can decode to the same value; which check compares bytes rather than values?
readings.introduction: Every parser that reads bytes from outside the process is attack surface: upload formats, binary protocols, compressed bodies, custom headers. Unit tests check the inputs you thought of. Go's built-in fuzzer mutates seed inputs, guided by coverage, to find the ones you did not, such as a length field that points past the end or a non-canonical encoding that breaks a round trip.
readings.nuance: A non-minimal varint parses without panicking and within limits, but re-encoding it yields different bytes, so only the round-trip comparison fails.
readings.objective: Write a native Go fuzz test with seed inputs and real invariants for a binary parser, harden the parser against what it finds, and cap decompressed size with io.LimitReader.
readings.question: Which invariant in a parser's fuzz target catches a non-canonical length encoding that the other checks miss?
readings.reviewAnswer: Encode(Parse(b)) equals b whenever Parse succeeds

sections.body: Parsers fail in a few recurring ways. They trust a declared length and slice past the end of the buffer, which in Go is a panic rather than memory corruption; but an unrecovered panic in a background goroutine stops the whole process, and even net/http, which recovers handler panics, drops the connection. They allocate whatever a length field asks for, so a five-byte message can request gigabytes. They accept several encodings of the same value, so two components that parse the same bytes disagree, which matters when one of them checks a signature or a policy. And decompressors turn a small input into a huge output. Each of these failures corresponds to an invariant a fuzzer can check on every input.
sections.title: Where parsers break

sections.body: The record format is a field count followed by tag, uvarint length and value for each field. Parse checks every length before slicing, caps the number and size of fields, rejects non-minimal varints and trailing bytes, and copies values so callers never alias the input buffer. The program runs Parse on the seeds a fuzz test would start from, shows the panic a naive parser hits, and inflates a gzip bomb through a size limit.
sections.title: A hardened parser, its seeds and a gzip bomb
sections.walkthrough: Seed 0 parses and re-encodes to identical bytes. Seed 1 declares five value bytes but carries two. Seed 2 encodes the length 0 as 0x80 0x00, which binary.Uvarint accepts but Encode never produces. Seed 3 asks for about four billion bytes and is refused before any allocation. Seed 4 has a trailing byte and seed 5 claims nine fields. naiveParse trusts the length, and the recovered panic shows the slice bound it hit. The bomb is 16 MiB of zeros that compresses to well under 64 KiB; readAtMost reads through io.LimitReader with limit+1 bytes, so it can tell a body exactly at the limit from one over it, and refuses the latter.

sections.body: A fuzz test is a function FuzzXxx(*testing.F) in a _test.go file. f.Add registers seed inputs, and f.Fuzz receives the target, whose parameters after *testing.T must match the seed types. The target does not know the right answer for a random input; it states what must hold for every input. For a parser, three invariants catch most bugs: it never panics, its output is bounded by its input and its limits, and a successful parse re-encodes to exactly the same bytes.
sections.title: The fuzz test: seeds plus invariants
sections.walkthrough: This _test.go fragment sits next to Parse and Encode in a package named record; run it with go test in your own environment. Without -fuzz, go test runs only the seeds and any files under testdata/fuzz/FuzzParse, so the fuzz test doubles as a cheap regression test. A panic anywhere in Parse fails the target, which is invariant one. The byte-count check fails if a bug ever reports more value bytes than were read. The round-trip check is the strongest of the three, and it holds only because Parse accepts canonical encodings alone.

sections.body: Fuzz one target at a time: -fuzz takes a regular expression that must match exactly one fuzz test in exactly one package. As an experiment, remove the non-minimal check from Parse and the matching seed from the test: on a laptop the fuzzer found the round-trip failure in under a second, minimized it, and wrote it to testdata/fuzz/FuzzParse, from where plain go test replays it. Commit those files; they are the regression tests for the bugs you fixed. Run the seeds on every commit, a short fuzzing budget on a schedule, and longer sessions after parser changes.
sections.code:
# Seeds and saved failures only, as in every CI run:
go test ./record -run=FuzzParse

# Generate new inputs for a fixed budget:
go test ./record -run='^$' -fuzz=FuzzParse -fuzztime=60s

# Replay one saved failure while fixing it:
go test ./record -run=FuzzParse/c8edd71d506c459a
sections.title: Run it and keep what it finds
sections.walkthrough: Run these in your own module. The first command replays seeds and saved corpus files without generating anything. The second fuzzes for 60 seconds across all CPUs; inputs that expand coverage are cached under $GOCACHE/fuzz, not in the repository. In the experiment the report read: round trip changed 01308000 into 013000, that is count 1, tag 0x30 and the two-byte encoding of length zero that Encode shortens to one byte. The saved file starts with the line go test fuzz v1 followed by the input as a Go literal; the hash in its name will differ on your machine.

sections.body: Limits belong at every layer that can expand data. http.MaxBytesReader caps the compressed request body, but a gzip body inflates after that check, so wrap the decompressor in a LimitReader as readAtMost does and treat hitting the limit as an error rather than silently truncating. The net/http Transport transparently decompresses gzip responses it asked for, so outbound response bodies need the same cap. For zip archives, the sizes in the headers are claims made by whoever built the archive: limit the number of entries and the bytes read per entry and in total, and leave entry names to the path-traversal lesson. Never preallocate from a declared length without a cap. Fuzzing proves nothing about inputs it never reached, so check the seed run with go test -coverprofile and add seeds for the branches it misses.
sections.title: Bound decompression and allocation everywhere

readings.takeaway: Give every parser of untrusted input a fuzz test with seeds and invariants (no panic, bounded output, canonical round trip), commit the failures it finds, and cap every declared length and every decompressed byte.
readings.title: Fuzz the parsers that read untrusted bytes, and bound what they may allocate or inflate
wrongAnswers: The parser returns an error instead of panicking
The number of fields stays below the configured limit

cautions: The checksum database proves consistency, not that code is benign.
Tool directives add tool dependencies to the application's module graph.
designGuide.cost: A govulncheck step and a build-information gate in CI, plus reviewer time for every dependency update; keeping the defaults on costs nothing.
strengths: Reachability analysis keeps vulnerability reports short and actionable.
Embedded build information makes every shipped binary auditable after the fact.

readings.hint: The database is a transparent log of hashes; think about what a hash can and cannot say about code.
readings.introduction: Most of the code in a Go binary was written by someone else. The toolchain provides strong defaults: go.sum pins exact module content, the checksum database exposes a module version that changed after publication, and every binary records the modules it was built from. Supply-chain security in Go is mostly about not weakening those defaults, and about reacting quickly and precisely when a dependency has a known vulnerability.
readings.nuance: The checksum database makes content tampering and per-user substitution detectable; whether the published code is safe still needs review and govulncheck.
readings.objective: Run govulncheck in CI, rely on go.sum and the checksum database correctly, pin tools with tool directives, build with -trimpath, and audit a binary's embedded build information.
readings.question: A new version of a dependency is listed in the Go checksum database. What does that establish?
readings.reviewAnswer: Everyone gets the same content for a module version

sections.body: govulncheck compares your dependencies, and the Go version itself, against the Go vulnerability database. In source mode it builds a call graph and reports a vulnerability as affecting you only when your code can reach a vulnerable function, which turns a long list of advisories into the few that matter now. Vulnerable modules that you import but never call are summarized separately. Binary mode inspects a compiled executable, which is the right check for what you actually ship, but it cannot show call stacks. Standard-library vulnerabilities are fixed by moving to a newer Go patch release, so scan with the same Go version you release with.
sections.code:
# Pin the scanner in go.mod (Go 1.24+), so developers and CI run one version:
go get -tool golang.org/x/vuln/cmd/govulncheck@latest

go tool govulncheck ./...                       # source mode: reachable findings
go tool govulncheck -show verbose ./...         # also list imported but unreached ones
go tool govulncheck -mode=binary ./bin/orders   # audit what you actually ship
sections.title: Report the vulnerabilities your code can reach
sections.walkthrough: Run these in your own module; govulncheck fetches advisories from the Go vulnerability database. go get -tool records the resolved version in go.mod and go.sum, and go tool runs exactly that version, building it on first use. In its default text output, govulncheck exits with a non-zero status when it finds vulnerabilities your code reaches, so a CI step fails on the findings that matter. Reachability is a static approximation: reflection and some indirect calls can hide a path, so schedule upgrades for unreached findings instead of ignoring them.

sections.body: go.sum records a hash of each module version's file tree and of its go.mod file. When the go command first downloads a module version that go.sum does not list, it checks the hash against sum.golang.org, a transparent log that lets every user confirm they see the same content for the same version. That defends against a compromised proxy or origin serving you different code from everyone else, and against a version tag moved after publication. It does not say the code is benign: a malicious version published openly is logged faithfully. Private modules must not be looked up in public services, which is what GOPRIVATE controls.
sections.code:
go env -w GOPRIVATE='*.corp.example.com'   # no public proxy or checksum DB for these
go mod verify                               # module cache still matches go.sum
go mod tidy -diff                           # non-zero exit if go.mod or go.sum would change
go build -mod=readonly -trimpath -o bin/orders ./cmd/orders
go version -m bin/orders                    # the embedded module and build record
sections.title: What go.sum and the checksum database prove
sections.walkthrough: Run these in your own environment. GOPRIVATE takes comma-separated glob patterns of module path prefixes and keeps those modules away from proxy.golang.org and sum.golang.org; GONOPROXY and GONOSUMDB override it for finer control. go mod verify detects tampering in the local module cache. go mod tidy -diff prints needed changes and exits non-zero, so CI catches a go.mod that drifted from the imports. -mod=readonly is already the default without a vendor directory, but stating it guards against a GOFLAGS=-mod=mod in the environment quietly rewriting requirements. -trimpath replaces file system paths with module paths, so binaries do not reveal the build machine's layout and are easier to reproduce.

sections.body: Tools that run in CI or through go generate, such as linters, code generators and govulncheck, execute with your repository's credentials, so they deserve the same pinning as libraries. Since Go 1.24 a tool directive in go.mod records each one: go tool runs it at the recorded version, go get tool upgrades every declared tool, and go install tool installs them into GOBIN. Tool dependencies join your module graph, which can raise shared dependency versions for the application too; if that is unwanted, declare the tools in a separate go.mod and pass -modfile to go tool. Avoid go install pkg@latest and download-and-run installers in CI scripts: they execute whatever was published most recently, unreviewed.
sections.title: Pin and review tools like code

sections.body: Every module-mode binary embeds its main module, its dependency versions with checksums, and build settings such as -trimpath, CGO_ENABLED and the VCS revision. go version -m prints that record, debug/buildinfo.ReadFile reads it from a file, and runtime/debug.ReadBuildInfo returns the running program's own copy. A release gate can read the candidate binary and refuse to ship it when the record shows a modified working tree or a dependency replaced by a local directory. The program applies such a policy to a fixed record and then prints only those fields of its own record that do not vary between environments.
sections.title: Audit what a binary was built from
sections.walkthrough: candidate mirrors what the go command records for a build from a modified checkout: since Go 1.24, go build appends +dirty to the main module version and sets vcs.modified=true. The replaced dependency carries no checksum because a directory has no published content to hash, which is exactly why it must not reach a release. audit walks Settings and Deps as slices, so findings print in a stable order. For the running program, ReadBuildInfo fills GoVersion from runtime.Version, and a program that imports only the standard library lists no dependency modules. Paths, VCS fields and target platform vary by environment, so they are not printed; go run does not stamp VCS information at all, while go build does.

sections.body: Each upgrade imports code that runs with your service's privileges. Update deliberately, one dependency or one related group per change, so a regression points at its cause. Read the go.mod and go.sum diff and look for modules that arrived transitively; go mod why -m explains why a module is needed and go mod graph shows who requires it. Skim the release notes and the size of the source diff in the upstream repository. Run the tests and govulncheck on the result. Automated update pull requests, such as Dependabot version updates for Go modules, are useful when a person reviews them with the same care as any other change. And prefer fewer dependencies: a small, well-understood helper is sometimes cheaper to own than a module that brings twenty more.
sections.code:
go list -m -u all                    # available upgrades appear in [brackets]
go get golang.org/x/net@v0.61.0 && go mod tidy
git diff go.mod go.sum               # new transitive modules show up here
go mod why -m golang.org/x/text      # which import path needs this module
go test ./... && go tool govulncheck ./...
sections.title: Review dependency updates as code changes
sections.walkthrough: Run these in your own module; the module and version are examples. go list -m -u all shows each module with any newer version in brackets. go get changes one requirement and go mod tidy settles the graph, after which the git diff of go.mod and go.sum is the review surface: every new line in go.sum is code you have not seen before. go mod why -m prints the shortest import path that needs the module. The last line gates the change on tests and reachable vulnerabilities, the same checks CI repeats.

readings.takeaway: Keep the toolchain's defaults on (go.sum, the checksum database, read-only module mode), gate CI on reachable govulncheck findings, pin tools in go.mod, and refuse releases whose embedded build information shows a dirty tree or a local replacement.
readings.title: Secure the Go supply chain: reachable vulnerabilities, verified modules, pinned tools, auditable binaries
wrongAnswers: The version was reviewed and contains no malware
The version has no known vulnerabilities

lessons.explanation: A signed token can be genuine and still belong to the wrong audience, issuer or operation. Even a fully valid token does not prove that its subject may read a particular order. Treat authentication as construction of a verified principal and authorization as an explicit resource-scoped decision. Fail closed when either contract is missing rather than accepting whatever identity-shaped value a request provides.
lessons.objective: Validate identity separately from permission to act on a particular resource.
lessons.title: Authentication and authorization: a verified token is only the beginning

lessons.explanation: A fast hash, password hash, MAC, encryption scheme and digital signature answer different questions. A SHA-256 digest does not make a password database resistant to guessing, and encryption without authentication can accept altered ciphertext. Use reviewed libraries and document the purpose, key lifetime, input format and resource budget before selecting a primitive.
lessons.objective: Choose purpose-specific primitives and bound their cost instead of inventing cryptography.
lessons.title: Passwords, MACs and randomness solve different problems

lessons.explanation: A URL supplied by a user can target internal services, metadata endpoints or a different host after redirection. Checking that the string begins with https is insufficient. Prefer a small configured set of upstream services and let user input select a resource within one of them. When arbitrary destinations are a real requirement, enforce address and egress policy at connection time as well as during URL parsing.
lessons.objective: Keep outbound destinations controlled and validate redirects and connection-time policy.
lessons.title: SSRF: let user input choose data, not an arbitrary network destination

lessons.explanation: A TLS connection can encrypt traffic to the wrong peer if verification is disabled. Certificate chain trust and hostname identity both matter; changing a boolean until a development request succeeds can silently remove production authentication. Use a deliberate trust store, keep the expected server identity tied to the configured destination and handle private development certificates through a separate test trust configuration.
lessons.objective: Keep certificate-chain and hostname verification while making trust and rotation explicit.
lessons.title: TLS: verify the peer instead of disabling the error

units.summary: Authentication and authorization, cryptographic purposes, controlled egress and TLS peer identity.
units.title: Service security foundations
units.translationNote: Apply these patterns in your own native services with an explicit threat model. These lessons do not introduce GopherForge accounts or registration.

lessons.explanation: SQL injection happens when a value supplied by a user becomes part of the statement the database parses. database/sql gives you a second channel: the query text reaches the driver as one string and every argument travels beside it as a typed value. The SQL rows lesson stated that placeholders bind values, not grammar; this lesson makes that separation visible with a recording driver and covers the places where binding alone is not enough: identifiers, sort direction and LIKE patterns.
lessons.objective: Send untrusted values as database/sql arguments, pick identifiers from allow-lists in code and escape LIKE wildcards with an explicit ESCAPE clause.
lessons.title: SQL injection: the query text and the user's values must reach the driver separately

lessons.explanation: Cross-site scripting happens when data from one user becomes markup or script in another user's browser. Escaping is the defense, but the correct escaping depends on where a value lands: a text node, a quoted attribute, a URL, a JavaScript string and a CSS value each have different metacharacters. Go's html/template parses your template, tracks that context at every action and applies the matching escaper automatically. text/template does none of this, and typed strings such as template.HTML tell html/template to stop.
lessons.objective: Render untrusted data with html/template, read its context-specific escaping and treat every typed-content conversion as a reviewed trust decision.
lessons.title: html/template escapes by context, and template.HTML is where that protection switches off

lessons.explanation: Cross-site request forgery abuses ambient credentials. A page on another site submits a form or calls fetch toward your service, the browser attaches your session cookie, and your handler sees an authenticated request it never meant to accept. Since Go 1.25 the standard library ships http.CrossOriginProtection, which rejects non-safe cross-origin browser requests using the Sec-Fetch-Site and Origin headers instead of a per-form secret. This lesson shows what that check decides, where SameSite fits and what stays your responsibility.
lessons.objective: Protect cookie-authenticated endpoints with net/http's CrossOriginProtection, know what SameSite cookies add and recognize when a synchronizer token is still required.
lessons.title: CSRF: reject cross-origin writes with Sec-Fetch-Site and http.CrossOriginProtection

lessons.explanation: A session cookie is a bearer credential: whoever presents it is the user until the server decides otherwise. Its attributes control where the browser sends it and whether page scripts can read it; the server-side record controls how long it is honored. Getting either half wrong produces familiar incidents: a cookie copied out by an injected script, a session an attacker fixed before the victim logged in, or a logout that only deleted the browser's copy.
lessons.objective: Issue a __Host- session cookie with the right attributes, rotate the ID at login and enforce idle, absolute and logout expiry in a server-side store.
lessons.title: Session cookies: lock down the attributes and keep the session's lifetime on the server

lessons.explanation: Path traversal turns a file name from a request into access somewhere else on disk: ../ segments, an absolute path or a symlink that leads out of the intended directory. The classic Go defense, filepath.Join plus Clean plus a prefix check, works on strings while the kernel resolves the real path later, symlinks included. Go 1.24 added os.Root, which opens a directory once and resolves every later name inside it, and Go 1.25 extended it with ReadFile, WriteFile, MkdirAll and other helpers.
lessons.objective: Open user-named files through os.Root, use filepath.IsLocal and Localize for early rejection and extract archives without zip-slip.
lessons.title: Path traversal: confine file access with os.Root, because Join and Clean only edit strings

lessons.explanation: Go's os/exec does not invoke a shell: exec.Command takes a program and an argument slice, so semicolons and $(...) inside an argument are ordinary bytes. The operations lessons on Bash arguments and safe CLIs already rely on that. This lesson covers the injection that survives without a shell: a user value read as an option by the target program, an operation chosen by the request, and a child process that inherits your environment and outlives its deadline.
lessons.objective: Start external tools with exec.CommandContext and a fixed argv, block argument injection with validation and --, and bound the child's time and environment.
lessons.title: Command injection: run tools without a shell and keep user input out of option position

lessons.explanation: Login, logout and OAuth flows often carry a next or return_to parameter. If the server redirects to whatever it contains, an attacker can send a link that starts on your trusted domain and ends on a lookalike login page, and in OAuth flows a redirect can leak codes or tokens. The obvious fix, allow only relative paths, is harder than it looks: browsers parse URLs by the WHATWG URL Standard, Go's net/url follows RFC 3986, and every difference between them is a bypass.
lessons.objective: Validate redirect targets so only same-site paths and allow-listed https URLs pass, including the //host, backslash and userinfo tricks that browsers and net/url read differently.
lessons.title: Open redirects: accept a single-slash path or an allow-listed host, not any URL that parses

lessons.explanation: Response headers turn browser features into policy: which scripts may run, whether the page may be framed, whether a response may be reinterpreted as another content type, how much of the URL leaks to other sites and whether plain HTTP is ever acceptable again. None of them fixes a bug in your handlers. They limit what an escaping mistake, an injected script or a hostile frame can do, so they belong in one middleware that wraps every response.
lessons.objective: Write middleware that sets a nonce-based Content-Security-Policy and the other baseline security headers, and roll them out without breaking pages or locking in HSTS preload by accident.
lessons.title: Security headers: a per-request CSP nonce, HSTS, nosniff, frame-ancestors and Referrer-Policy

units.summary: SQL injection, XSS, CSRF, session cookies, path traversal, command injection, open redirects and security headers.
units.title: Web application security
units.translationNote: Each attack is shown against a local model and fixed with the standard library. Test only systems you own or are authorized to assess.

lessons.explanation: Most leaked credentials are not stolen from a vault; they are printed. A startup line that logs the configuration with %+v, an error that wraps a connection string, a debug endpoint that dumps settings: each copies the secret into log storage that more people can read, for longer, than the secret store itself. Make printing safe by default and make revealing the value an explicit, searchable call.
lessons.objective: Wrap credentials in a Secret type that redacts itself in fmt, slog and JSON, redact credentials in URLs, and load secrets with errors that name the source but never the value.
lessons.title: Keep secrets out of logs and errors with a type that refuses to print itself

lessons.explanation: A comparison that stops at the first differing byte takes longer the more of the guess is correct. Against a token, an API key or a MAC tag, that turns an impossible search over the whole value into a byte-by-byte search an attacker can run with enough repeated requests. Constant time here means time that depends only on public facts, such as the length, and never on the contents of the secret.
lessons.objective: Recognize timing-dependent comparisons and replace them with crypto/subtle or hmac.Equal over fixed-size digests, including the lookup and error paths around them.
lessons.title: Compare secrets in constant time: an early return reveals how much of a guess was right

lessons.explanation: Encrypting a column protects data in backups, replicas and database dumps, but only if the record format answers more than which key to use. The crypto-purposes lesson explains why encryption must be authenticated. This lesson builds the record envelope: AES-GCM through crypto/cipher, a fresh random nonce per seal, a key ID that survives rotation, and additional data that ties each ciphertext to the row it belongs to.
lessons.objective: Seal application records with AES-GCM so that tampering, row swapping and key rotation are handled explicitly, and explain why a repeated nonce breaks GCM.
lessons.title: Encrypt records with AES-GCM: random nonces, a key ID, and the record ID as additional data

lessons.explanation: The crypto-purposes lesson establishes that passwords need a slow, salted, memory-hard function. The operational questions come next: how to store the parameters with each hash so they can change later, how to upgrade old hashes without forcing resets, how to budget memory when many users log in at once, and how to keep the login endpoint from telling an attacker which accounts exist.
lessons.objective: Hash passwords with argon2id in a self-describing PHC-style string, upgrade parameters at login, handle bcrypt's 72-byte limit and keep login failures indistinguishable.
lessons.title: Store passwords with argon2id: encoded parameters, rehash on login, one answer for every failure

lessons.explanation: The identity-authorization lesson says to validate a token's full contract before trusting the principal it names. This lesson designs the tokens themselves. Opaque tokens are random strings that mean nothing without a lookup, so revocation is immediate. Signed tokens carry their claims and verify without a lookup, so revocation is hard and every claim check is your job. Both need expiry, rotation and a plan for theft.
lessons.objective: Choose between opaque and signed tokens, store opaque tokens as hashes with rotation and reuse detection, and verify HMAC-signed JWTs with a pinned algorithm and checked claims.
lessons.title: Design tokens deliberately: hashed opaque tokens, strictly verified signed tokens, expiry and rotation

lessons.explanation: Every parser that reads bytes from outside the process is attack surface: upload formats, binary protocols, compressed bodies, custom headers. Unit tests check the inputs you thought of. Go's built-in fuzzer mutates seed inputs, guided by coverage, to find the ones you did not, such as a length field that points past the end or a non-canonical encoding that breaks a round trip.
lessons.objective: Write a native Go fuzz test with seed inputs and real invariants for a binary parser, harden the parser against what it finds, and cap decompressed size with io.LimitReader.
lessons.title: Fuzz the parsers that read untrusted bytes, and bound what they may allocate or inflate

lessons.explanation: Most of the code in a Go binary was written by someone else. The toolchain provides strong defaults: go.sum pins exact module content, the checksum database exposes a module version that changed after publication, and every binary records the modules it was built from. Supply-chain security in Go is mostly about not weakening those defaults, and about reacting quickly and precisely when a dependency has a known vulnerability.
lessons.objective: Run govulncheck in CI, rely on go.sum and the checksum database correctly, pin tools with tool directives, build with -trimpath, and audit a binary's embedded build information.
lessons.title: Secure the Go supply chain: reachable vulnerabilities, verified modules, pinned tools, auditable binaries
